title: AP Macroeconomics
summary: Work through national output, inflation, stabilisation and international finance with explicit model assumptions.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 6 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review.

modules.title: Scarcity and comparative advantage
modules.focus: Calculate opportunity costs before recommending specialisation.
explanation: Scarcity requires choices because resources have alternative uses. Opportunity cost is the next-best option forgone. A production possibilities frontier shows combinations feasible with given resources and technology; points inside indicate unused or inefficiently allocated capacity.

Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, not greater total output. Mutually beneficial exchange can occur when a trading price lies between the participants’ opportunity costs, even if one has an absolute advantage in both goods.

workedExample.prompt: One worker can make 12 bowls or 6 plates; another can make 8 bowls or 8 plates.
steps: The first gives up 2 bowls per plate; the second gives up 1 bowl.
The second has comparative advantage in plates; the first in bowls.

misconception.claim: The more productive worker has comparative advantage in everything.
misconception.correction: Relative opportunity costs determine comparative advantage.

questions.prompt: A producer makes either 20 loaves or 5 cakes. What is one cake’s opportunity cost?
questions.answer: Four loaves per cake.

questions.prompt: Does moving from inside to on a frontier necessarily mean economic growth?
questions.answer: No. It can mean using existing resources better; growth shifts productive capacity outward.

questions.hint: Ask what is forgone when choosing one additional unit.
questions.prompt: A producer can make 24 units of X or 8 of Y. Find the opportunity cost of one Y and of one X.
questions.answer: One Y costs 3 X; one X costs 1/3 Y.
checkpoints: Take the reciprocal for X cost.
Attach the correct good units to each result.
hints: Ask what is forgone when choosing one additional unit.
The two costs use different units.

questions.hint: Separate actual production from potential production.
questions.prompt: An economy moves from an interior point to its existing frontier after unemployed workers find jobs. Is this necessarily an outward shift of productive capacity?
questions.answer: No. Output rises through greater use of existing resources; an outward shift would require increased resources, improved technology or another capacity change.
checkpoints: Distinguish movement to the frontier from a shift.
hints: Separate actual production from potential production.
The stated frontier has not changed.

notes.title: Reasoning through scarcity and comparative advantage
paragraphs: Scarcity forces choices even when resources are used efficiently. A production possibilities frontier separates feasible combinations from combinations unavailable with the current resources and technology. Moving towards the frontier uses idle resources; shifting the frontier outward represents greater productive capacity. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, not on producing the greatest absolute quantity. To evaluate possible trade, compute each producer’s cost of one good in units of the other and seek a trading price between their costs. Specialisation can expand consumption possibilities, but the simple model does not establish how gains are distributed or account for every transition cost.

workedExamples.prompt: Country A can produce 30 units of grain or 10 cloth; B can produce 20 grain or 20 cloth. Identify comparative advantages and a mutually beneficial grain price for one cloth.
steps: A’s cloth costs 3 grain; B’s cloth costs 1 grain. B has comparative advantage in cloth and A in grain.
A price of 2 grain per cloth lies between 1 and 3: B receives more grain than its opportunity cost and A pays less than its own cost.
workedExamples.conclusion: The proposed trade ratio of 2 grain per cloth can benefit both in this model.

flashcards.front: What determines comparative advantage?
flashcards.back: Lower opportunity cost.

flashcards.front: Does absolute advantage guarantee comparative advantage in every good?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: What does moving from inside to the frontier show?
flashcards.back: More complete resource use.

flashcards.front: What bounds a mutually beneficial trade ratio?
flashcards.back: The two opportunity costs in the simple two-producer model.

modules.title: Output, prices and unemployment
modules.focus: Separate nominal measures from real change.
explanation: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services produced domestically during a period. It excludes intermediate goods to avoid double counting. Nominal GDP uses current prices, while real GDP controls for price changes.

The unemployment rate divides unemployed job-seekers by the labour force. People outside the labour force are excluded. Inflation measures the rate of increase in a price index, so a falling inflation rate can still mean prices are rising.

workedExample.prompt: A price index rises from 125 to 130. Calculate inflation.
steps: Find the increase: 130 − 125 = 5.
Divide by the initial index: 5 ÷ 125 × 100 = 4%.

misconception.claim: Lower inflation means the price level fell.
misconception.correction: Prices fall only when the inflation rate is negative over the measured period.

questions.prompt: A labour force has 190 employed and 10 unemployed people. Find unemployment.
Nominal GDP rises 8% while the price level rises. Can real growth be assumed to be 8%?
questions.answer: No. Some nominal increase reflects higher prices; real growth requires a constant-price measure.

questions.hint: The index-point change is not the percentage change.
questions.prompt: A price index rises from 160 to 168. Find inflation.
checkpoints: Use the initial index as denominator.
hints: The index-point change is not the percentage change.
Divide by 160, not 168.

questions.prompt: A population has 900 employed, 100 unemployed and 500 outside the labour force. Find the unemployment rate.
questions.answer: The labour force is 1000, so unemployment is 100/1000×100=10%; the 500 outside it are excluded from this denominator.
checkpoints: Add employed and unemployed to find 1000.
Divide unemployed by the labour force.
Explain why the outside group is excluded.
hints: Use the defined labour-force population.
Do not divide by all 1500 people.

notes.title: Reasoning through output, prices and unemployment
paragraphs: GDP measures the market value of final production within an economy over a period, avoiding double counting of intermediate goods. Nominal GDP uses current prices, whereas real GDP holds prices constant using a specified measurement method to isolate output change. A price index compares a basket or aggregate across periods; its level is not the inflation rate. The unemployment rate uses unemployed people actively seeking and available for work as a share of the labour force in the simplified definition. People outside the labour force are not automatically counted as unemployed, so a falling rate alone need not indicate improving employment.

workedExamples.prompt: An economy produces 100 units at price 2 in year 1 and 120 at price 3 in year 2. Using year-1 prices, calculate nominal and real GDP growth.
steps: Nominal GDP rises from 200 to 360, an 80% increase.
Real GDP rises from 200 to 240 at the base price, a 20% increase; the rest of the nominal change reflects price changes and their interaction.
workedExamples.conclusion: Nominal growth is 80%, while real output growth is 20%.

flashcards.front: What does real GDP seek to isolate?
flashcards.back: Changes in production rather than prices.

flashcards.front: Is an index level of 140 an inflation rate of 140%?
flashcards.back: No; inflation is the percentage change in the index.

flashcards.front: What is the labour-force denominator?
flashcards.back: Employed plus unemployed people meeting the definition.

flashcards.front: Why exclude intermediate goods from final expenditure GDP?
flashcards.back: To avoid double counting their value.

modules.title: Aggregate demand and short-run output
modules.focus: Trace spending changes through the multiplier and AD–AS model.
explanation: Aggregate demand combines consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports. A change in planned spending shifts AD; a change in the overall price level moves along it. Short-run output can depart from potential output when wages and other costs adjust slowly.

In a simple closed model without taxes or imports, the spending multiplier is 1/(1 − MPC). Real economies have additional leakages, price responses and capacity limits, so the simple calculation is conditional.

workedExample.prompt: With MPC = 0.75, government purchases increase by 20 in the simple model.
steps: The multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.
The model predicts an eventual output increase of 80, holding prices and other assumptions fixed.

misconception.claim: Any government purchase increase raises real GDP by the simple multiplier in all conditions.
misconception.correction: Leakages, crowding out and price adjustment can change the actual effect.

questions.prompt: With MPC = 0.8, what is the simple spending multiplier?
What happens initially after a negative supply shock in AD–AS?
questions.answer: The price level rises and real output falls, with AD held constant.

questions.prompt: With MPC=0.50 in the simple spending model, how much autonomous spending closes an output gap of 80?
questions.answer: The multiplier is 2, so required autonomous spending is 80/2=40.
checkpoints: Divide the desired output change by it.
hints: Solve ΔY=kΔA for ΔA.
Do not multiply the gap by the multiplier.

questions.hint: The shock acts directly on production costs.
questions.prompt: An oil-price increase raises firms’ production costs. In a basic AD–AS model, identify the initial curve shift and likely price/output directions.
questions.answer: Short-run aggregate supply shifts left; the price level rises and real output falls, holding aggregate demand unchanged.
checkpoints: Identify higher costs as an SRAS shift.
Give higher prices and lower output with AD held fixed.
hints: The shock acts directly on production costs.
Trace the new intersection with unchanged demand.

notes.title: Reasoning through aggregate demand and short-run output
paragraphs: Aggregate demand combines planned spending on domestic output by households, firms, government and foreign buyers net of imports. A shift in aggregate demand changes short-run output and the price level depending on aggregate supply conditions. In the simple fixed-price expenditure model, an initial spending change creates successive income and consumption rounds; the multiplier is 1/(1−MPC) only under its stated assumptions. Taxes, imports, interest-rate responses and capacity constraints can reduce or alter that result. A supply shock differs from a demand shift: higher production costs can raise prices while reducing short-run output, creating a policy trade-off.

workedExamples.prompt: In a simple fixed-price model with MPC=0.60 and no taxes or imports, autonomous investment rises by 30. Find the total output change and the first two induced consumption rounds.
steps: The multiplier is 1/(1−0.60)=2.5, so ΔY=2.5×30=75.
The first induced consumption round is 18 and the next is 10.8; later rounds form a declining geometric series.
workedExamples.conclusion: The model predicts an output increase of 75, with induced rounds 18 and 10.8 initially.

flashcards.front: What does MPC measure?
flashcards.back: The fraction of additional disposable income consumed.

flashcards.front: What is the simple spending multiplier?
flashcards.back: 1/(1−MPC) under the model assumptions.

flashcards.front: What does a negative supply shock do initially?
flashcards.back: It can lower output while raising the price level.

flashcards.front: Why is the simple multiplier conditional?
flashcards.back: Leakages, prices, rates and capacity can change the response.

modules.title: Money, banks and interest rates
modules.focus: Connect monetary policy to borrowing and spending.
explanation: Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Financial assets differ in liquidity and return. A bond’s fixed payments become less attractive when market interest rates rise, so its price tends to fall.

Monetary policy influences financial conditions and spending. Distinguish models with scarce reserves from ample-reserves frameworks; a mechanical deposit multiplier is a simplified upper-bound exercise, not a prediction of how all modern banks lend.

workedExample.prompt: A bond pays a fixed 50 each year. Its price falls from 1,000 to 800.
steps: The simple current yield starts at 50 ÷ 1,000 = 5%.
At 800 it becomes 6.25%, illustrating the inverse price–yield relationship.

misconception.claim: A bond’s price and yield always move in the same direction.
misconception.correction: For fixed promised payments, a lower purchase price implies a higher yield.

questions.prompt: Why might lower borrowing rates increase investment?
questions.answer: Projects with expected returns above the reduced financing cost become more attractive, other conditions unchanged.

questions.prompt: Expected inflation is 3% and the nominal rate is 7%. Approximate the real rate.
questions.answer: About 4% using the standard approximation.

questions.hint: Yield uses gain divided by purchase price.
questions.prompt: A one-year bond pays 1100 at maturity and costs 1000. If its price rises to 1050 with payment unchanged, compare yields.
questions.answer: The original yield is 10%; the new yield is 50/1050≈4.76%, so the higher price lowers yield.
hints: Yield uses gain divided by purchase price.
The final payment stays fixed.

questions.hint: Nominal positivity does not ensure real positivity.
questions.prompt: A nominal interest rate is 4% and expected inflation is 6%. Find the approximate real rate and interpret it.
questions.answer: The approximate real rate is −2%; the monetary return is expected to buy less after inflation, despite a positive nominal payment.
hints: Nominal positivity does not ensure real positivity.
Compare money growth with price growth.

notes.title: Reasoning through money, banks and interest rates
paragraphs: Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value, but its purchasing power can change with prices. Financial assets differ in liquidity and risk, so a bond is not identical to transaction money. A fixed-payment bond’s price and yield move inversely: paying less for the same promised payment raises the yield measure. Nominal interest rates describe monetary payments, while real rates adjust for inflation; expected inflation matters for decisions made in advance. Bank lending involves balance-sheet changes and constraints, so a simple reserve-multiplier exercise should not be treated as a complete description of modern lending or monetary policy.

workedExamples.prompt: A one-year bond pays 1050 at maturity and sells for 1000 today. Find its nominal yield and approximate real yield if expected inflation is 2%.
steps: Approximate real yield is 5%−2%=3%; the exact purchasing-power adjustment is 1.05/1.02−1≈2.94%.
workedExamples.conclusion: Nominal yield is 5%, with an approximate real yield of 3%.

flashcards.front: What are three functions of money?
flashcards.back: Medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.

flashcards.front: How do fixed-payment bond price and yield relate?
flashcards.back: Inversely.

flashcards.front: What is the approximate real interest rate?
flashcards.back: Nominal rate minus inflation.

flashcards.front: Why use expected inflation for an advance decision?
flashcards.back: Actual future inflation is not yet known.

modules.title: Stabilisation, inflation and growth
modules.focus: Separate short-run demand effects from productive capacity.
explanation: Demand stimulus can reduce a recessionary gap in the short run. If output exceeds potential, rising wages and costs can shift short-run aggregate supply left until output returns towards potential, with a higher price level.

Long-run growth comes from productive resources, technology and institutions, not simply higher spending. Borrowing-financed deficits may raise interest rates and crowd out private investment in the loanable-funds model, with effects depending on conditions and policy responses.

workedExample.prompt: An economy at potential receives a persistent increase in aggregate demand.
steps: Initially, real output and the price level may rise in the sticky-cost model.
As costs adjust, output returns towards potential while the price level remains higher.

misconception.claim: The short-run inflation–unemployment trade-off is permanent.
misconception.correction: Expectations and supply conditions shift the short-run relationship; it is not a stable long-run menu.

questions.prompt: How can improved education support long-run growth?
questions.answer: Greater human capital can raise output per worker and productive capacity, though quality and use of skills matter.

questions.prompt: Why can government borrowing reduce private investment in a basic model?
questions.answer: More demand for loanable funds can raise real interest rates, making some private projects unprofitable.

questions.hint: Compare income after tax under flexible and fixed tax payments.
questions.prompt: During a downturn, tax payments fall under existing income-tax rules. Explain how this can stabilise disposable income without a new policy vote.
questions.answer: Lower tax payments partly cushion the fall in household disposable income, supporting consumption relative to a fixed-tax scenario; the response follows existing rules.
checkpoints: Connect it to spending without new discretionary legislation.
hints: Compare income after tax under flexible and fixed tax payments.
The rule changes the payment automatically.

questions.hint: Trace which side of the model changes.
questions.prompt: A country raises spending but makes no lasting change in labour, capital or technology. Does the basic model imply permanently higher potential output?
questions.answer: No. Demand can affect actual output, but potential output requires changes in productive capacity; temporary stimulus alone does not establish such a change.
checkpoints: Name a capacity condition needed for a lasting potential-output claim.
hints: Trace which side of the model changes.
Higher spending does not itself prove higher capacity.

notes.title: Reasoning through stabilisation, inflation and growth
paragraphs: Stabilisation policy seeks to reduce fluctuations around sustainable output, but timing, expectations and supply conditions affect its impact. Expansionary demand policy can raise output when unused capacity exists; near potential output, more of the effect may appear in prices. Automatic stabilisers respond through existing rules as income changes, whereas discretionary measures require new decisions. Long-run growth depends on productive capacity, including capital, skills, technology and institutions, rather than a permanent sequence of demand boosts alone. Government borrowing can affect interest rates and private investment in a loanable-funds model, although the size and direction of effects depend on wider conditions.

workedExamples.prompt: In a simple loanable-funds graph, government borrowing increases while private saving supply is unchanged. Trace the predicted interest-rate and investment effects.
steps: Additional borrowing shifts demand for loanable funds right, raising the equilibrium real interest rate in the model.
At the higher rate, some private investment projects no longer meet their required return, so private investment can fall.
workedExamples.conclusion: The model predicts upward pressure on real rates and possible crowding out of private investment.

flashcards.front: What is an automatic stabiliser?
flashcards.back: A fiscal mechanism that changes with income under existing rules.

flashcards.front: Why can demand stimulus raise prices near capacity?
flashcards.back: Output has less room to expand.

flashcards.front: What supports long-run productive growth?
flashcards.back: Capital, skills, technology and other capacity improvements.

flashcards.front: What does crowding out describe?
flashcards.back: Reduced private activity associated with government borrowing or spending through an identified mechanism.

modules.title: Exchange rates and international flows
modules.focus: Track currency demand before predicting appreciation.
explanation: An exchange rate is one currency’s price in terms of another. Appreciation makes foreign goods cheaper for domestic buyers and domestic goods more expensive for foreigners, other things equal. State the quotation before interpreting a movement.

International transactions connect trade and financial flows. Higher domestic returns can attract financial inflows, increasing demand for domestic currency. Exchange-rate effects on trade also depend on contracts, responsiveness and other economic changes.

workedExample.prompt: One domestic currency unit buys 0.8 foreign units, then 1.0 foreign unit.
steps: The domestic currency appreciates because each unit buys more foreign currency.
A foreign item priced at 80 foreign units costs 100 domestic units initially and 80 afterwards.

misconception.claim: A larger numerical exchange rate always means depreciation.
misconception.correction: The interpretation depends on which currency is in the numerator.

questions.prompt: How might domestic appreciation affect exports, other things equal?
questions.hint: Think from a foreign buyer’s perspective.
questions.answer: Domestic goods become more expensive in foreign currency, tending to reduce quantity demanded.

questions.prompt: Why might higher domestic interest rates increase currency demand?
questions.answer: Investors seeking higher returns may buy domestic currency to purchase domestic assets.

questions.prompt: One domestic unit buys 0.50 foreign units, then 0.60. Find the percentage change and identify appreciation or depreciation.
questions.answer: The domestic currency appreciates by (0.60−0.50)/0.50×100=20% in this quotation.
checkpoints: Identify more foreign currency per domestic unit.
Use the initial quote as denominator.
hints: Read the quote’s units first.
The domestic unit’s foreign purchasing power rises.

questions.hint: Multiply the domestic price by foreign units per domestic unit.
questions.prompt: A domestic good costs 100 domestic units. The exchange rate rises from 0.8 to 1.0 foreign units per domestic unit. Find its foreign price and explain the possible export effect.
questions.answer: Its foreign price rises from 80 to 100 foreign units. With other conditions unchanged, the higher price can reduce foreign demand for the good.
checkpoints: Link the increase to possible lower demand, conditionally.
hints: Multiply the domestic price by foreign units per domestic unit.
Do not assert that quantities change mechanically without demand response.

notes.title: Reasoning through exchange rates and international flows
paragraphs: An exchange rate must be read with its units. If one domestic currency unit buys more foreign currency, the domestic currency appreciates; the reciprocal quotation moves in the opposite numerical direction. Appreciation can make foreign goods cheaper for domestic buyers and domestic goods more expensive for foreigners, other things equal. Trade volumes also depend on contracts, demand responses and production conditions, so exchange-rate direction does not guarantee an immediate trade-balance change. Financial flows can respond to expected returns, risk and future exchange-rate expectations. Balance-of-payments categories record transactions, not a simple ranking of whether an economy is doing well.

workedExamples.prompt: An exchange rate changes from 2 domestic units per foreign unit to 2.5. A foreign item costs 40 foreign units. Find its domestic price before and after, and identify the currency movement.
steps: The item costs 80 domestic units initially and 100 afterwards.
More domestic currency is needed for one foreign unit, so the domestic currency depreciates; the domestic price rises 25%.
workedExamples.conclusion: The item’s domestic price rises from 80 to 100 as the domestic currency depreciates.

flashcards.front: What is domestic appreciation in foreign-units-per-domestic-unit terms?
flashcards.back: The quoted number rises.

flashcards.front: What happens to the reciprocal quote?
flashcards.back: It falls.

flashcards.front: Why might depreciation support exports?
flashcards.back: Domestic goods can become cheaper in foreign-currency terms, other things equal.

flashcards.front: Why can interest-rate differences fail to predict currency flows alone?
flashcards.back: Risk and expected future exchange rates also affect returns.
